title: PrivEscalate: Measuring and Augmenting the Threat of LLM-Automated Linux Privilege Escalation

questions.question: How many Dockerized scenarios and sub-categories does the PrivEscalate benchmark comprise, and how many parameterized variants does it add?
questions.answer: 531 audited Docker-based Linux privilege-escalation scenarios spanning a 14-subcategory taxonomy, plus 329 parameterized perturbation variants generated by altering environmental elements of selected original scenarios.

questions.question: What three findings emerge from evaluating six LLMs across three agent architectures?
questions.answer: (i) Model capability is heterogeneous across vulnerability classes, with no single model dominating the high-prevalence classes; (ii) LLM successes are sensitive to environmental perturbation (per-model retention 59.0%–78.2%), so configuration rotation disrupts some exploit attempts but does not eliminate the measured risk; (iii) Agent architectures can materially change success rates and reorder model rankings, with model-dependent magnitude.

questions.question: What is PrivEscAgent and which modules does it add to the ReAct base agent?
questions.answer: A domain-specialized wrapper that augments the generic (wintermute) ReAct agent with four modules: PrivEnum (deterministic, LLM-free enumeration in a single shell round-trip), CategoryMatcher (two-tier rule-based plus LLM-assisted ATT&CK category classification), StrategySelector (ranks candidates by confidence weighted by per-category success-rate priors and auto-pivots on failure), and StepPlanner (decomposes multi-step exploits into verifiable steps with rollback).

questions.question: Which model leads the overall success rate in RQ1, and which model leads the Sudo misconfiguration class?
questions.answer: GPT-5.4 (reasoning-augmented) leads overall SR with 40.9% and SUID/SGID abuse with 45.8%, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.7% overall) leads Sudo misconfiguration with 46.1%.

questions.question: Which LLM backed all stages of the benchmark construction pipeline, and what did the construction cost?
questions.answer: Claude Opus 4.6 was the backing LLM for all pipeline stages. The recorded construction logs total $1,044 in API cost, and among verified scenarios with cost logs the mean generation-and-verification cost is $0.76 per scenario.

questions.question: What five transformation axes are used to create the perturbed variant scenarios?
questions.answer: (1) Credentials: changed username, password, and root password; (2) System identity: different hostname; (3) Enumeration noise: 3 non-exploitable SUID binaries, 2 decoy user accounts, and 2 harmless cron entries; (4) Context noise: a custom MOTD banner and pre-seeded misleading shell history; (5) Environment fingerprint: pre-installing additional common network/file-inspection utilities.

questions.question: How does the HackSynth architecture change the aggregate model ranking relative to wintermute?
questions.answer: Under HackSynth the ranking flips: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (66.5%) now leads GPT-5.4 (47.3%) by 19.2 pp, the opposite of their wintermute ordering. HackSynth improves five models (largest gains for Claude Sonnet 4.6 +28.8 pp, Qwen-Plus +14.7 pp, Claude Haiku 4.5 +10.6 pp, GPT-4.1 +7.2 pp) but falls below wintermute for DeepSeek v3.2 (−7.7 pp).

questions.question: What experimental configuration (step budget, temperature, interface) is used for the evaluations?
questions.answer: Zero-knowledge conditions with max 20 steps per attempt, temperature 0, and an SSH interface; the agent starts from a low-privilege SSH foothold and must reach uid=0(root) with no hints about the vulnerability category or exploitation method.

questions.question: How was benchmark quality audited and with what outcome?
questions.answer: A stratified sample of 82 of the 525 pipeline/seed scenarios (±10% margin of error at 95% confidence) was independently graded by two auditors trained by a five-year offensive-security expert, then adjudicated. After adjudication, 79/82 (96.3%) had verified Dockerfile correctness and 80 (97.6%) verified exploit validity; overall 2 scenarios were removed and 9 sub-category labels corrected, yielding the final 531-scenario set.

questions.question: Which failure mode dominates failed runs, and which model is the Loop outlier?
questions.answer: Wrong-method dominates failures (81.6% weighted average across the six models; exploit attempts issued but failing to reach root). Qwen-Plus is the clear Loop outlier at 15.1% versus ≤2.2% for the other five models.

questions.question: In the ablation study, which PrivEscAgent module is the most consistent contributor?
questions.answer: PrivEnum: removing it causes the largest SR drop for the five non-reasoning models, ranging from −5.3 to −19.2 pp. By contrast, removing StepPlanner hurts Claude Sonnet 4.6 (−7.5 pp) and Qwen-Plus (−11.4 pp) but actually improves GPT-5.4.

questions.question: How does PrivEscAgent affect per-success cost relative to the baselines?
questions.answer: It lowers per-success cost relative to HackSynth for all six models and relative to wintermute for five models; the exception is DeepSeek v3.2 (+200% vs its already very low wintermute cost). For example, GPT-5.4 costs $0.14 per success (−89% vs wintermute, −91% vs HackSynth).
